desc: Long-form techno and house tracks with Karl Hyde's stream-of-consciousness vocals, including the epic "Pearl's Girl".
Trio blending rap, soul and reggae, featuring Lauryn Hill's cover of "Killing Me Softly".
Song cycle of violent folk-style narratives, with duets featuring Kylie Minogue and PJ Harvey.
Cinematic noir instrumentals and songs for imaginary films, with guest vocals from Jarvis Cocker and Nick Cave.
Instrumental album constructed entirely from samples of obscure vinyl records.
Debut of jazz-tinged piano songs sung in a deep, smoky voice, including "Criminal".
Debut of literate, softly sung indie pop originally pressed in a small run as a college project.
Dub-heavy, paranoid electronic rock conceived as an alternative soundtrack to the 1971 film Vanishing Point.
Carey's turn toward hip hop-influenced R&B with collaborators including Puff Daddy and Bone Thugs-n-Harmony.
Funky, film-soundtrack-style breakbeat album woven with field recordings of New York street voices.
Organ-led, Stones-influenced Britpop recorded around the death of keyboardist Rob Collins.
Debut mixing reggae, soul and trip-hop textures, including the single "Even After All".
Mix of Punjabi influences, indie pop and dance beats, featuring the hit "Brimful of Asha".
Droning, psychedelic alt-rock from Portland, including the ironic hit "Not If You Pay Me".
Second album broadening the band's punky Britpop with more varied, piano-touched arrangements.
Debut built on Timbaland's skittering, sparse productions and Missy Elliott's quirky flows.
Murky, blues-based songs of aging and loss produced by Daniel Lanois.
Veteran Cuban musicians recorded in Havana with Ry Cooder, reviving pre-revolution son and bolero.
Raw, filtered house debut built on looped samples, including "Around the World" and "Da Funk".
Expansive drone rock layered with gospel choirs, orchestra and free jazz horns, about heartbreak and addiction.
Solo debut of the former Take That singer, featuring the ballad "Angels".
String-laden anthems and ballads including "Bitter Sweet Symphony" and "The Drugs Don't Work".
Quiet, jazz-inflected songs with contributions from Brian Eno and Paul Weller.
Seven love songs crooned by Neil Hannon over a full orchestra, recorded live.
Interlocking twin guitars, no bass, and dual shouted vocals in a fierce, tightly wound punk record.
Jazz-inflected drum and bass with live double bass and vocals, winner of the 1997 Mercury Prize.
Sparse, piano-led love songs and meditations on faith and heartbreak.
Heavy breakbeats and psychedelic samples, including "Block Rockin' Beats" and "Setting Sun".
Hushed, double-tracked vocals and intricate acoustic guitar on songs of addiction and despair.
Punk-attitude electronic album with "Firestarter", "Breathe" and "Smack My Bitch Up".
Rawer, American lo-fi-influenced turn away from Britpop, including "Song 2" and "Beetlebum".
Layered guitar rock exploring technology, alienation and modern life, including "Paranoid Android".
Rap-rock party album mixing hip hop, metal and southern rock, including "Bawitdaba".
Down-tuned, hip hop-inflected metal with slap bass, including "Freak on a Leash".
Unrecorded Woody Guthrie lyrics set to new music by Billy Bragg and Wilco.
1966 concert, actually recorded in Manchester, with an acoustic set then a loud electric set with the Hawks.
Southern road songs of memory and longing in a weathered, rootsy rock setting.
Tabla-driven fusion of Indian classical music and drum and bass, winner of the 1999 Mercury Prize.
Electronica-infused pop produced with William Orbit, reflecting on motherhood and spirituality.
Bleak, cinematic follow-up to fame, exploring aging, excess and pornography.
Lush, fragile orchestral psych-pop recorded in the Catskills with guests from The Band.
Home-recorded acoustic songs over programmed beats, including "Babylon" and "This Year's Love".
Riff-heavy, provocatively camp punk rock with glam and hard rock swagger.
Polished, California-themed alternative rock co-written in part with Billy Corgan.
Lo-fi multilingual songs about migration and borders, recorded on travels across Latin America.
Blend of rap, soul and doo-wop on love and faith, linked by classroom interludes.
Sample-packed big beat including "The Rockafeller Skank", "Praise You" and "Right Here, Right Now".
Retro-futuristic downtempo using vintage synths and vocoder, including "Sexy Boy" and "La femme d'argent".
Warped analogue synths, hip hop beats and children's voices evoking faded 1970s memories.
Repetitive, groove-locked guitar riffs from former Kyuss guitarist Josh Homme.
Frantic, politically charged metal with Armenian folk melodies and sudden shifts in tempo.
Modern raï from the Algerian singer, blending North African vocals with pop and western production.
Debut built on Max Martin-produced pop hooks, led by the title single.
Melodic alternative rock with turntable textures, including the acoustic single "Drive".
Nine-piece masked band's punishing debut, with extra percussion, samples and screamed vocals.
Melodic guitar pop from Liverpool's Head brothers, steeped in Love and 1960s songwriting.
Eclectic house debut mixing ragga, Latin and funk, including "Red Alert" and "Rendez-Vu".
Folk-rooted songs with soft electronic touches, including "Stolen Car".
Stuart Price's pastiche of 1980s electro-funk and synth-pop, featuring a guest vocal from Nik Kershaw.
Stark, quiet songs about death and darkness from Will Oldham, including the title track.
Major-label debut introducing Eminem's violent, comic Slim Shady alter ego, produced largely by Dr. Dre.
Blend of Indian classical, flamenco and electronica exploring identity and nuclear testing.
Heavy alternative rock driven by Skin's powerful vocals, mixing ballads and metallic riffs.
Live recording of Metallica performing with the San Francisco Symphony, arranged by Michael Kamen.
Orchestral and acoustic songs, including "River of Orchids", after years of record-label dispute.
Melodic comeback with John Frusciante back on guitar, including "Scar Tissue" and "Otherside".
Kathleen Hanna's lo-fi electro-punk debut with sampled beats and feminist lyrics, including "Deceptacon".
Dark, psychedelic electronic rock with guests including Iggy Pop and Bobby Gillespie.
Three-volume set of 69 songs about love in many genres, written by Stephin Merritt.
Gentle, melodic guitar ballads produced by Nigel Godrich, including "Why Does It Always Rain on Me?".
Slow, glacial post-rock with falsetto vocals in Icelandic and bowed guitar.
Electronic tracks built around vintage blues and gospel field recordings, every song licensed for commercial use.
Symphonic, studio-crafted psych-pop about mortality and science, with heavy, processed drums.
Chart-topping rap-metal album including "Rollin'" and "My Way".
Glitchy electro-pop produced largely by Mirwais, with a country and western visual aesthetic.
Howe Gelb's loose, desert-tinged alternative country rock.
Return to melodic guitar rock produced by Eno and Lanois, including "Beautiful Day".
Debut pairing rapped and screamed vocals over polished metal riffs, including "In the End".
Experimental, politically minded hip hop with sci-fi themes and electronic production.
Cinematic downtempo debut evoking 1960s film scores, with Alison Goldfrapp's dramatic vocals.
Elliott Smith's most ornately arranged album, with Beatles-influenced melodies and layered harmonies.
Sparse, acoustic breakup record, with Emmylou Harris singing harmony on "Oh My Sweet Carolina".
Soul-inflected chamber country with Kurt Wagner singing in a falsetto.
Understated, guitar-led debut including "Yellow" and "Trouble".
Atmospheric, mostly self-written songs set in moody, Lanois-style production.
Soft bossa nova vocals over subtle electronic beats, produced partly by Suba.
Confessional, controversial follow-up including "Stan", "The Real Slim Shady" and "The Way I Am".
Serbian producer Suba's mix of Brazilian sounds and electronics, released after his death in a studio fire.
Classically trained producer's polished 2-step garage, including "Crazy Love" and "Sincere".
Soulquarians-produced hip hop with live instrumentation, including "The Light".
Warmer, live-band neo soul on relationships and society, including "Bag Lady".
German cabaret singer performs songs written for her by Tom Waits, Elvis Costello, Neil Hannon and others.
Continuous collage of thousands of samples forming a seamless, nostalgic dance record.
Sprawling, homespun singer-songwriter debut that won the 2000 Mercury Prize.
Mostly instrumental score for Sofia Coppola's film, with hazy 1970s-style prog textures.
Polished, New York-inspired rock album with a Thom Yorke duet, winner of the 2001 Mercury Prize.
Atmospheric, brooding guitar rock debut from former dance act Sub Sub.
Live-band blend of jazz, breakbeat and trip hop built around upright bass.
Shift toward electronics, ambient and jazz textures, with obscured, processed vocals.
Genre-mixing Atlanta hip hop with funk, rock and drum and bass, including "B.O.B." and "Ms. Jackson".
Spare duo recordings by Gillian Welch and David Rawlings, centered on acoustic guitars and close harmony.
David Berman's dry, poetic songs in a country-leaning indie rock setting.
Empowerment-themed R&B including "Survivor", "Bootylicious" and "Independent Women".
Double concept album about the American South and the story of Lynyrd Skynyrd.
1960s Los Angeles garage-psych, named after their hit with its backwards and fuzz guitar.
Warm, melodic downtempo debut including "Eple", "Poor Leno" and "Remind Me".
Stripped-down guitar-and-drums duo record including "Fell in Love with a Girl" and "We're Going to Be Friends".
Cartoon-band debut from Damon Albarn and Jamie Hewlett, mixing dub, hip hop and pop.
Tango bandoneon and strings set over downtempo electronic beats.
Recorded alongside Kid A, closing with the New Orleans jazz-inflected "Life in a Glasshouse".
Laid-back mix of folk, hip hop beats and psychedelia, including "Squares".
Short, lean guitar-rock debut with distorted vocals and interlocking guitars, including "Last Nite".
Genre-hopping Welsh psych-pop also released as a surround-sound DVD with videos for every song.
Soul-sample-driven production by Kanye West and Just Blaze, including "Izzo (H.O.V.A.)" and "Takeover".
Hushed, domestic album of microbeats, harp, music boxes and choir.
Compilation of fast, sharp garage punk including "Hate to Say I Told You So".
Personal, genre-spanning pop record including "Beautiful" and "Dirrty".
Solo debut produced by The Neptunes and Timbaland, including "Cry Me a River" and "Rock Your Body".
Garage, R&B and hip hop with socially conscious lyrics, winner of the 2002 Mercury Prize.
Long, conversational songs with spoken-word passages, reissued with a restored running order.
Reunion with the E Street Band reflecting on the aftermath of September 11.
Piano-driven second album including "Clocks", "The Scientist" and "In My Place".
Late-career Rick Rubin production of covers and originals, including Nine Inch Nails' "Hurt".
Soft, intimate debut mixing jazz, folk and country, including "Don't Know Why".
Short, fuzzed-out garage rock debut alternating loud punk bursts with Beatlesque ballads.
Somber, orchestrated breakup album produced by Nigel Godrich.
Home-recorded, retro-leaning mix of psych, soul and Latin grooves.
Debut mixing 1960s Merseybeat, sea shanties and psychedelia, including "Dreaming of You".
Expansive guitar rock including "There Goes the Fear" and "Pounding".
Rootsy songs fractured by static and electronic textures, initially rejected by the band's label.
Live-band hip hop branching into rock and soul, including "The Seed 2.0".
Group-rap trade-offs over turntable-heavy, old-school production from Cut Chemist and DJ Nu-Mark.
Electronic-leaning psych-pop about mortality and love, including "Do You Realize??".
Southwestern border music mixing alt-country, mariachi horns and cinematic instrumentals.
Lavish orchestral pop with operatic arrangements and introspective lyrics.
Irish band's Beach Boys-influenced debut fixated on California.
Concept album of complex, Latin-inflected prog rock about a man in a drug-induced coma.
Analogue-recorded blues rock including "Seven Nation Army" and its bass-like guitar riff.
